question: An 8-month-old breastfed infant of a strict vegan mother presents with macrocytic anaemia and developmental regression. Serum B12 is 80 pg/mL (low), serum folate is normal. Which management is most appropriate?

answers.text: Start folic acid 1 mg/day immediately to correct the macrocytic anaemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Folic acid alone is contraindicated when B12 deficiency is confirmed. It will correct anaemia but worsen neurological B12 deficiency, risking irreversible subacute combined degeneration.

answers.text: Start vitamin B12 (hydroxocobalamin) IM and defer folate until B12 stores are replete

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. With confirmed B12 deficiency (low B12, normal folate), treat with IM hydroxocobalamin first. Neurological recovery requires adequate B12; folic acid alone would worsen subacute combined degeneration.

answers.text: Reassure and supplement with dietary cow's milk to provide both B12 and folate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dietary advice is a prevention measure, not an acute treatment. The infant has established B12 deficiency with developmental regression requiring immediate parenteral B12 therapy.

answers.text: Start both B12 and folate simultaneously in full doses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While this avoids the risk of folate-only treatment, the preferred approach when B12 deficiency is confirmed is to start B12 first. Giving folate simultaneously is acceptable only if B12 is given concurrently.

overallFeedback.feedback: With confirmed low B12 and normal folate, start vitamin B12 (IM hydroxocobalamin) first. Folic acid alone risks worsening neurological B12 deficiency and is contraindicated in this setting.
Correct! B12-before-folate is the critical rule. IM hydroxocobalamin is the treatment of choice for infantile B12 deficiency with neurological involvement.
